content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studied federated bilevel optimization problems with a nonconvex upper level and strongly convex lower level. Authors proposed two algorithms, FedBiO and its accelerated variant FedBiOAcc, to solve this problem. Authors provided the computation and communication complexities of proposed algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The story of the paper is relatively complete, from elementary algorithm to its acceleration, and finally the experiment for a verification.

Weakness:
1. The motivation of the study can be further strengthened.
2. The writing of the paper can be further polished to be more organized.
3. The comparison with existing works seems to be not sufficient, which makes me confused on the significance of the work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the main techniques are not that novel, the acceleration strategies have already been studied in related bilevel literature. The writing of the paper can be further enhanced to improve the clarity of the paper, and highlight the significance of results.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My main concerns here are the significance of the results. Simple research shows that there are some closely related works (3 months before ICLR submission deadline), for example:

- Tarzanagh, Davoud Ataee, et al. "FEDNEST: Federated Bilevel, Minimax, and Compositional Optimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.02215 (2022).
- Chen, Xuxing, Minhui Huang, and Shiqian Ma. "Decentralized bilevel optimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.05670 (2022).
- Yang, Shuoguang, Xuezhou Zhang, and Mengdi Wang. "Decentralized gossip-based stochastic bilevel optimization over communication networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.10870 (2022).

They also studied the problem with the nonconvex and stronlgy-convex setting. With that I am confused on the significance of the paper. I suggest authors try to incorporate these papers into your submission, and further highlight the significance of your results.

Another point is the writing of the submission, to be honest, I feel a bit sloppy on the flow of the paper. For example, authors introduced "two types of errors" at the introduction (beginning of Page 2), then discuss it again in Section 4 (end of Page 5), which is redundant. Also I suggest authors leverage paragraphs and subtitles to better organize those lengthy text in one single paragraph. The writing now seems to be in a rush.

I don't have enough time to go through the lengthy proof regarding the short reviewing time frame. But I believe the complexity resutls here should be reasonable. I hope to learn more from authors on the insights of the paper. Thank you very much for the efforts.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides an analysis of local stochastic bilevel optimization. Two algorithms are provided, including FedBiO and FedBioAcc, where FedBiO is based on a deterministic gradient oracle while FedBioAcc is based on a stochastic gradient oracle. Communication and computational complexies are provided. The authors also conducted fair federated learning experiments to test the proposed algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
S1: The literature review is sufficient. 
S2: The proposed algorithm is new.

Weaknesses
W1: The convergence analysis of FedBiO is very weak. A standard parallel implementation of ATD-BiO or ITD-BiO with instant communication among clients in [Reference1] would result in $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ computation and $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ communication complexity. This result dominates Theorem 5.1 of this paper. The current version of this paper does not cite [Reference1]; please cite this paper and add enough discussions since this is a very relevant baseline. 

[Reference1] Ji, Kaiyi, Junjie Yang, and Yingbin Liang. "Bilevel optimization: Convergence analysis and enhanced design." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.

W2: The Theorem 5.2 does not imply convergence and the implications of the Theorem 5.2 is wrong. From the complete statement of Theorem 10.1 (page 44 in the appendix), the learning rate $\eta$ is of order $I^2$ and $I=T^{1/3}M^{-2/3}$ (in Remark 6). Note that the constant $M'$ in Theorem 5.2 (page 8) has $1/\eta$ dependency, so the RHS of the Theorem 5.2 is not going to zero. The statement of the linear speedup in the Remark 6 is also problematic. The authors did not take the order of $M'$ into account.

W3: It is unclear what is the real technical contribution of this paper since most analysis seems to be from existing results (e.g., momentum-based variance reduction from [Cutosky and Orabona, 2019], the bilevel techniques from [Ji et al. 2021]).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Low to Medium. Readers can understand what the algorithm and the convergence results are, but the discussions with prior work are missing so it is difficult to see what is the real contribution compared with previous work.

Quality and Novelty: Low. The convergence results are either trivial (Theorem 5.1) or problematic (Theorem 5.2). It is unclear what is the new technical insights from the proofs.

Reproducibility: Medium. No code is provided, although some description is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes and analyzes two new algorithms, FedBiO and FedBiOAcc, with convergence analysis. However, one theorem does not have improved complexity results and another theorem is problematic. Therefore I vote for rejecting this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the federated bilevel problem, where each client has to solve an inner problem, and the outer problem is an average of the clients outer loss -- that depends on the solution to the inner problem. For this problem, the authors first propose FedBio, a bilevel extension of FedAvg, which uses full batch updates and does periodic average of the outer variable. In the stochastic case, the authors then propose FedBioAcc that uses momentum based variance reduction to achieve better convergence rates. The authors then prove that the complexity of FedBio and FedBioAcc is  $\varepsilon^{-1.5}$, but FedBioAcc has a lower $\varepsilon^{-1}$ communication complexity. The authors then perform an experiment of group fair learning, where the objective is to learn a new weight for each training sample. The weights are learned such that the test loss over all clients is minimized.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths:

- This paper studies an original problem. To the best of my knowledge, it is the first to study this specific formulation of federated bilevel where each client has their own inner problem and where the outer problem is shared.
- FedBioAcc reaches the same complexity as single level federated algorithms in a non convex setting.

# Weaknesses:

- The authors do not seem to release any code here, which greatly diminishes the reproducibility of this work.

- The experimental validation could be improved. First, the authors compare their methods to non-bilevel methods like fedavg: it would be greatly beneficial to explain what exactly is implemented here (we cannot look at the code since the code is not provided). What optimization problem do these methods solve? Second, table.1 displays the final metrics obtained with the different methods. FedBIO and FedBioAcc are supposed to solve the exact same optimization problems, FedBioAcc should just be faster. Why do we get such a discrepancy between their metrics in the end ? This does not make much sense to me. Also, a figure which shows the evolution of metrics like test Acc and test EqOpp over time would nicely complement this table.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# Clarity:
- The paper is well written and easy to understand.
- The experiments section could be made clearer for instance by clearly specifying which problem the authors are trying to solve with each algorithm.

# Quality:
 
- The theoretical part of the paper is of great quality: it studies an original and interesting problem, and the authors provide algorithms that are optimal to solve it.
- As explained above, the theoretical evaluation is lacking.

# Novelty

- This work is novel and timely


# Minor comments:
- The word 'federated' is very important in this work, it should probably be in the title.
- There are several relevant works that could be worth mentioning. For instance, [1] is also proposing federated bilevel, with a different formulation (in this paper, the inner is also shared by clients). There are several missing references regarding stochastic bilevel algorithms, including [3], which achieves a $\varepsilon^{-1}$ error with a stochastic algorithm and [4] which uses the same variance reduction technique as in this paper. [4] is a relevant reference regarding convergence rate of federated learning in non-convex settings.
- In the appendix sec 11, the formulation of the bilevel problem seems to be exactly that of data hypercleaning: can the authors elaborate on this ?
- The authors cite Khanduri et al. 21 as a reference for federated learning results while this is a bilevel paper that never deals with federated learning
- Since FedBio is not a stochastic algorithm, it would be nice to mention the sample complexity as well. It would also be interesting to study a stochastic version without acceleration.
- Table 1 overlaps with the text.


[1]: Tarzanagh, Davoud Ataee, et al. "FEDNEST: Federated Bilevel, Minimax, and Compositional Optimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.02215 (2022).

[2]: Dagréou, Mathieu, et al. "A framework for bilevel optimization that enables stochastic and global variance reduction algorithms." arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.13409 (2022).

[3]: Li, Junyi, Bin Gu, and Heng Huang. "A fully single loop algorithm for bilevel optimization without hessian inverse." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 36. No. 7. 2022.

[4]: Das, Rudrajit, et al. "Faster non-convex federated learning via global and local momentum." Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence. PMLR, 2022.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a well written paper that studies a timely and novel problem. The authors propose algorithms to efficiently solve the problem, and FedAccBio reaches the same complexity as single level federated learning. The only problem is the experimental validation, which is not clear enough, and the code is not released.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper consider distributed bilevel optimization. The authors propose two momentum-based algorithms to solve deterministic and stochastic distributed bilevel optimization, and derive their convergence rates. The authors also conduct numerical experiments to test the algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

1. The authors apply the momentum method to distributed bilevel optimization and establish the current best sample complexities under this setting. 

Weakness: 

1. The novelty of this paper is limited. There has been some works in distributed bilevel optimization [1], which established the convergence results without variance reduction. Meanwhile, momentum has also been applied to stochastic bilevel optimization and established the $O(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ sample complexity in the non-distributed setting [2]. It seems not challenging to apply the existing momentum bilevel methods with existing distributed bilevel optimization models. Thus, the novelty and contributions seems to be marginal. 

2. In remark 5, the rate for deterministic distributed problem is slower than that for nondistributed problems, and the authors claim that this is because of the effect of consensus. Is it because of the problem itself that each machine has its own inner problem or other reasons? Meanwhile, as the central machine collects the information from all other machines in each round, it is unclear why the $\epsilon$ term within the convergence rate would be effected. It would be helpful if the authors could provide some intuition to explain why the convergence rate is slowed down in this case.

3.  The linear speedup argument in Theorem 5.2 seems to be wrong. In Lemma 7, it can be seen that the convergence of $y_t^m$ would not be affected by $M$. However,  Theorem 5.2 makes the conclusion that the overall convergence speeds up w.r.t. $M$. It would be beneficial to explain why this would work and point out which lemma supports this argument. Actually, the convergence rate in Theorem 10.1 depends on the $\frac{\delta^3 \ln(T)}{\eta \sigma^2}$ term as well (see the second line of the equation within Theorem 10.1). As $\delta^3 = M^2$, multiplying this term to the $L_h(MT)^{-2/3}$ term, the convergence indeed slows down w.r.t. $M$, leading to a contradiction. 

4. In the numerical part, both FedBiO and FedBioAcc are tested on the same dataset. However, this is a bit confusing because FedBiO is designed for solving deterministic bilevel optimization problems but FedBiOAcc solves the stochastic case. It is unclear how the experiments are conducted. Meanwhile, it lacks comparison between the proposed algorithms and existing benchmarks. It would be helpful if additional numerical experiments can be provided to show their efficiency. 

References

[1] Tarzanagh, D. A., Li, M., Thrampoulidis, C., & Oymak, S. (2022). FEDNEST: Federated Bilevel, Minimax, and Compositional Optimization

[2] Prashant Khanduri, Siliang Zeng, Mingyi Hong, Hoi-To Wai, Zhaoran Wang, and Zhuoran Yang. 2021, A near-optimal algorithm for stochastic bilevel optimization via double-momentum.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper does not propose new formulations but considers an existing problem. It solves the problem with some well-understood variance reduction technique. The novelty is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper studies distributed bilevel optimization problem and applies momentum for acceleration. The extension from the nondistributed bilevel problem to distributed problem seems not challenging and the technical analysis is routine. The proofs are not well-explained and there are some potential faults within the paper. As a result, some theoretical claims might be wrong. In the numerical part, there is no comparison between the proposed algorithms with existing benchmarks. Overall, I cannot see too much new insights from this paper, in both theoretical and numerical aspects. The contributions seems to be incremental.

content.title: Local Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with Momentum-Based Variance Reduction
content.abstract: Bilevel Optimization has witnessed notable progress recently with new emerging efficient algorithms and has been applied to many machine learning tasks such as data cleaning, few-shot learning, and neural architecture search. However, little attention has been paid to solving the bilevel problems under distributed setting. Federated learning (FL) is an emerging paradigm which solves machine learning tasks over distributed-located data. FL problems are challenging to solve due to the heterogeneity and communication bottleneck. However, it is unclear how these challenges will affect the convergence of Bilevel Optimization algorithms. In this paper, we study Federated Bilevel Optimization problems. Specifically, we first propose the FedBiO, a deterministic gradient-based algorithm and we show it requires $O(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ number of steps/communication steps to reach an $\epsilon$-stationary point. Then we propose FedBiOAcc to accelerate FedBiO with the momentum-based variance-reduction technique under the stochastic scenario. We show FedBiOAcc needs $O(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ number of steps and $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ communication steps, this matches the best known rate for single-level stochastic federated algorithms. Finally, we validate our proposed algorithms via the important Fair Federated Learning task. More specifically, we define a bilevel-based group fair FL objective. Our algorithms show superior performances compared to other baselines in numerical experiments.
